reference: No. Overall, there was a poor knowledge of the side effects of ACE-I. This may account for the increased referrals for chronic cough and angioedema.

response:
Based on the provided context, visual loss in amblyopia is not necessarily permanent. One study reported that in 12 cases of patients with amblyopia, there was an improvement in distance and near visual acuity by 3.3 and 1.9 lines logMAR respectively within 12 months, with the improvement generally occurring between 1 and 12 months and remaining stable thereafter. Additionally, another study showed that after six months of treatment (including full refractive correction and occlusion therapy), the mean visual acuity of amblyopic eyes significantly improved from 0.35 ± 0.3 to 0.16 ± 0.2 logMAR (p < 0.001).

Therefore, amblyopic visual loss can improve with appropriate treatment, indicating it is not always permanent.
reference: No. Older people with a history of amblyopia who develop visual loss in the previously normal eye can experience recovery of visual function in the amblyopic eye over a period of time. This recovery in visual function occurs in the wake of visual loss in the fellow eye and the improvement appears to be sustained.
